dy5ro2L7hkM.title: Lindsay Clancy Wants A NOT GUILTY Verdict Without A New Trial
dy5ro2L7hkM.description:
Lindsay Clancy's first trial ended without a verdict. Now her defense is asking Judge Sullivan to enter a finding of not guilty himself. Kevin Reddington argues that prosecutors failed to present sufficient evidence to prove the underlying charges beyond a reasonable doubt—and separately argues that the state failed to overcome Clancy's lack-of-criminal-responsibility defense. It's an attempt to end the case without waiting for another jury.  

I walk through Reddington's argument and explain the enormous problem I see with it. The first trial was fought primarily over Lindsay Clancy's mental state, with the defense relying on lack of criminal responsibility. Now Reddington is attacking whether the state sufficiently proved the underlying conduct in the first place. I explain why that creates a major tension with how the defense tried the case, what the legal standard actually requires, and whether Judge Sullivan could really enter a not-guilty finding after the mistrial.

j4qCWU_clDE.title: Does Lindsay Clancy’s Lawyer WANT A New Judge?
j4qCWU_clDE.description:
I'm watching a potentially important timing fight develop in the Lindsay Clancy retrial. Judge William Sullivan made clear that he wants the case moving and specifically referenced getting it tried before his retirement. But when the court pushed for a trial date, Kevin Reddington said he cannot do the trial before June. That's significant because Sullivan reaches Massachusetts' mandatory judicial retirement age in June.   

I break down why I don't think that timing should be ignored. If Sullivan retires before the retrial can be completed, another judge could end up handling the case—and that could reopen important questions involving evidence, witnesses, and other trial rulings. I'll also show you the courtroom exchange that led me to ask whether Reddington would actually prefer another judge. That's my interpretation of the strategy, not something Reddington expressly admitted.

7Zl_lAyUY4k.title: Supreme Court Just BLOCKED Missouri’s New Election Map
7Zl_lAyUY4k.description:
Missouri's congressional map fight just flipped again. The Eighth Circuit had ordered federal courts to require use of Missouri's newer 2025 congressional map—the same map used during the August primary. But the Supreme Court has now stayed those orders, leaving the 2022 map in place for the 2026 congressional election unless the Court later changes course. The Court emphasized that ballots using the old map had already been printed and mailed, absentee voting was underway, and switching maps again in the middle of an election could create “electoral chaos.” Supreme Court

I go through the Supreme Court's ruling and explain why the Eighth Circuit's constitutional argument didn't carry the day. The appeals court had concluded that using one congressional map for the primary and another for the general violated Article I, Section 2. The Supreme Court said its precedents have not established that rule and focused heavily on the timing of the federal intervention and the Purcell principle against federal courts changing election rules when voting is already underway. I also explain how Missouri managed to conduct its primary under one map while now preparing to conduct the general election under another.

DYkZkR_csrg.title: Supreme Court Just REVIVED Trump’s Voter Citizenship Checks
DYkZkR_csrg.description:
The Supreme Court just handed the Trump administration an important interim victory over its modified SAVE program, allowing DHS to continue using expanded federal data—including Social Security Administration records—to help state and local authorities verify citizenship status while the litigation continues. The Court concluded that the government's legal position is likely to succeed, while Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson dissented with Justices Sonia Sotomayor and Elena Kagan and argued that the expanded system risks burdening lawful voters, including recently naturalized citizens. Legal Information Institute

I go through the ruling and then focus on something that jumped out at me in Justice Jackson's dissent: the way she repeatedly relies on her own prior dissenting opinions while arguing against the Court's decision here. I explain the difference between controlling majority precedent and a dissent, why citing a dissent isn't inherently improper, and why I found the repeated pattern in this particular opinion so striking. I also break down what the Court actually decided about SAVE—and what remains unresolved because this is a stay proceeding rather than the final judgment in the case.
